blocks.text: 1. R-Squared

blocks.alt: A model produces R-Squared, showing variance explained

blocks.text: MAE, MSE, and RMSE, all already covered in their own topics, each measure raw prediction error in some form. R-Squared answers a genuinely different question about a regression model's quality entirely.
It measures how much of the outcome's variation does the model genuinely explain, a genuinely different framing explored in full depth throughout this topic.
2. The Limitation Of Raw Error Alone

blocks.alt: A raw error number has no context on its own

blocks.text: This connects back to MAE, MSE, and RMSE, already covered as raw error metrics. A raw error value alone gives no genuine sense of whether that error is good or bad without additional context.
An RMSE of 5 could be genuinely excellent or genuinely terrible, entirely depending on context, such as whether the outcome being predicted typically ranges in the tens or in the millions.
3. R-Squared's Core Idea

blocks.alt: A model is compared against a naive mean baseline

blocks.text: R-Squared's genuinely core idea compares the model's own errors against a genuinely naive baseline: always predicting the average, regardless of any input features at all.
This gives a genuinely relative, context-aware measure rather than a raw, absolute error number, directly addressing the limitation already covered in the previous section.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Term","Meaning"],"rows":[["Naive baseline","A model that always predicts the average outcome, regardless of inputs"],["R-Squared","A relative measure comparing the model's errors against that naive baseline"]]}

blocks.text: 4. The Formula, Conceptually
This connects back to MSE, already covered in its own topic. R-Squared equals one minus the ratio of the model's own error to the naive baseline's error, both already covered in the previous section.
Both errors get measured using the same sum of squared errors already familiar from MSE, giving R-Squared a genuinely direct mathematical link to that earlier, more familiar metric.
5. Interpreting The Scale

blocks.alt: R-Squared of 1 is a perfect fit while R-Squared of 0 is no better than the mean

blocks.text: A genuinely intuitive scale governs R-Squared's values. An R-Squared of 1.0 means the model genuinely explains all of the outcome's variation, a perfect fit with zero remaining error.
An R-Squared of 0.0 means the model performs no better than the naive baseline, already covered in this topic, providing genuinely no improvement over simply guessing the average every time.
6. Negative R-Squared Values

blocks.alt: A model worse than the mean produces a negative R-Squared

blocks.text: A genuinely important, real edge case follows. This connects back to the naive baseline, already covered in this topic. R-Squared can genuinely go negative, a result that can surprise newcomers.
This means the model performs genuinely worse than simply predicting the average every time, a real, possible outcome for a genuinely poorly fit or badly overfit model evaluated on new data.

blocks.title: warning
blocks.content: A negative R-Squared, already covered in this topic, is a genuinely serious warning sign. It typically indicates the model is badly misspecified or severely overfit to data unlike what it is now being evaluated on.

blocks.text: 7. The Percentage-Of-Variance Framing

blocks.alt: R-Squared of 0.8 means 80 percent of variance explained

blocks.text: A genuinely popular, intuitive framing describes R-Squared values as percentages. An R-Squared of 0.75 is often described as the model explaining 75 percent of the outcome's variation.
This framing, already covered as popular in this section, makes R-Squared genuinely easy to communicate to audiences unfamiliar with the underlying formula already covered earlier in this topic.
8. A Genuine Limitation With Adding Features

blocks.alt: Adding any feature means R-Squared never decreases

blocks.text: A genuinely real limitation applies here. This connects back to Overfitting, already covered in its own topic. R-Squared alone can genuinely increase just from adding more features, even irrelevant ones.

This makes plain R-Squared a genuinely unreliable signal for comparing models with different numbers of features, since it can reward complexity, already covered as a risk factor for overfitting, rather than genuine explanatory power.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When R-Squared Is Genuinely The Right Metric

Explaining regression model quality to a genuinely non-technical audience is a direct case for R-Squared, since its percentage-of-variance framing, already covered, is genuinely intuitive and easy to communicate.

Comparing how well genuinely different models explain the same outcome is another genuine case where R-Squared, already covered, gives a genuinely direct, comparable answer, keeping the feature-count caveat already covered in mind.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates computing R-Squared for a genuinely simple regression model, comparing its errors against the naive baseline already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

true_values = np.array([10.0, 12.0, 15.0, 18.0, 20.0, 22.0, 25.0])
predictions = np.array([11.0, 13.0, 14.5, 17.5, 20.5, 21.0, 24.0])

r_squared = r2_score(true_values, predictions)

naive_baseline_prediction = np.full_like(true_values, true_values.mean())  # already covered as the naive baseline in this topic
baseline_error = np.sum((true_values - naive_baseline_prediction) ** 2)
model_error = np.sum((true_values - predictions) ** 2)

print(f"Model's sum of squared errors: {model_error:.3f}")
print(f"Naive baseline's sum of squared errors: {baseline_error:.3f}")
print(f"R-Squared (via scikit-learn): {r_squared:.4f}")
print(f"R-Squared (computed manually, already covered as the formula in this topic): {1 - model_error / baseline_error:.4f}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example confirms the manually computed R-Squared matches scikit-learn's own built-in calculation exactly, verifying the formula already covered as this topic's own core idea.

blocks.text: 11. Evaluation Metrics: Module Complete

items: R-Squared measures how much of the outcome's variation a regression model genuinely explains.
It compares the model's own errors against a naive baseline that always predicts the average.
An R-Squared of 1.0 means a perfect fit; 0.0 means no better than the naive baseline.
R-Squared can go negative, meaning the model performs worse than the naive baseline.
It is commonly framed as a percentage of the outcome's variation explained.
Plain R-Squared can increase just from adding more features, even irrelevant ones.
It is especially valuable for communicating model quality to non-technical audiences.
